newsitem.title: USA: U.S. thinks N.Korea nuke deal still makes sense.
newsitem.headline: U.S. thinks N.Korea nuke deal still makes sense.

text.p: The United States believes it still makes sense to go forward with a nuclear deal with Pyongyang despite a North Korean submarine incursion into the South, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said Tuesday.

"We think the nuclear agreement is an extremely important agreement," Christopher said. "It remains in the interests of both countries and indeed the region as a whole ... for North Korea not to go ahead with a nuclear programme."
"We would expect to maintain that freeze and maintain the framework," Christopher told reporters before a meeting with South Korean Foreign Minister Gong Ro-mung.

Under the October 1994 nuclear deal, Pyongyang agreed to halt its nuclear programme, thought by U.S. intelligence to have created enough plutonium for one to two weapons, in return for supply of modern reactors less able to produce nuclear fuel.

After the meeting, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Christopher expressed strong support for Seoul over the submarine affair to counteract widespread media reports last week that he had urged "all parties" to show restraint.

In last Wednesday's incident, the Northern submarine dropped some 26 commandos on a Southern beach in what South Korean President Kim Young-sam called a military provocation. The submarine grounded on the South Korean coast.

Burns said that because of the incident, the Clinton administration had persuaded Representative Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat who sometimes acts as an unofficial envoy abroad, to postpone a trip he had planned to North Korea last week.
"We just felt it was very important not to send a signal to North Korea of business as usual," Burns said.
Despite the anger the incident has created in Seoul, Gong told reporters his government had not yet decided whether to ask the United States to resume annual joint military exercises in the South.
South Korea's Defence Ministry said on Tuesday that Seoul would seek to restart the Team Spirit exercises, which were dropped last year as part of the landmark nuclear deal.

"To my knowledge, we haven't requested resumption of this joint military manoeuvre yet," Gong said. "I think this has to be first decided within the government and then I think we have to make consultations with the United States, if we so decide."

Burns said Gong later told Christopher that South Korea planned to introduce a U.N. Security Council resolution condemning North Korea over the incident. Christopher promised U.S. backing for the resolution, he said.

Burns said Washington shared Seoul's view that North Korea's claim that its submarine had drifted into Southern waters due to engine trouble was false. South Korean experts had found that the engine was in full working order, he said.
Despite the tensions created by the submarine affair, Christopher told reporters the nuclear deal was going well.

He said almost half of North Korea's spent fuel had been safely stored and an international consortium had raised more than $90 million from 20 countries toward the new reactors, whose main costs will be borne by South Korea and Japan.

In addition, Burns said Congress told the administration Tuesday that it would approve the full $25 million needed to cover the U.S. part of the deal, which involves supplying North Korea with heavy fuel oil.
Earlier, President Bill Clinton said in a speech to the U.N. General assembly that following North Korea's "provocative actions", it was important to pursue a peace for all Koreans.

North Korea has yet to respond definitively to a proposal launched in April by Clinton and Kim for four-party talks on a permanent settlement to the 1950-53 Korean War, which was ended by an armistice.
Like Clinton, Christopher and Gong were in New York to attend the current U.N. General Assembly session.
